card.name: Ula
card.tagline: Ancient Tongan group dance of converging lines and subtle hand gestures
card.profile: The ula is an ancient group dance from the Kingdom of Tonga, traditionally performed by women and girls following an ʻotuhaka. Recorded by European navigators including Captain Cook during eighteenth-century contact, it was historically the premier women's dance across the islands. Following the arrival of Christian missionaries, the Tongan royal family dramatically transformed the tradition, exchanging its original fast pace and full-body hip articulations for restrained, conservative carriage. Today, the dance retains its hallmark spatial split, where dancers enter from opposite wings and converge into lines while articulating refined gestures of the hands and head.
card.insight: Witnessed by Captain Cook before Christianity arrived, the once-frenetic Tongan ula was stripped of hip action by royalty, leaving girls in red to carry all meaning through hand and head movements.

card.profile_long:
The ula represents one of the oldest surviving dance traditions of Tonga, occupying a foundational place in Polynesian movement history before being eclipsed by its descendant, the tauʻolunga. When eighteenth-century European explorers, most notably Captain James Cook, made landfall in the Tongan archipelago, they documented the ula as an established group performance. In its pre-Christian context, the ula was the primary dance form performed by women, characterized by a rapid tempo and expressive, vigorous movement that actively engaged the hips, legs, feet, and upper torso. The arrival of Christian missionaries in the nineteenth century prompted a complete stylistic overhaul sanctioned by the Tongan royal family. Seeking alignment with conservative standards of comportment, the court re-engineered the choreography into a deliberately restrained, stiffened presentation, suppressing the energetic hip movements and establishing the modest aesthetic that persists into modern times.

Known alternatively as fahaʻi-ula or the 'split dance,' the execution of the tradition is defined by its distinctive staging and entrance choreography. Performers are almost exclusively girls, with male participation occurring only on rare occasions. To begin the performance, the ensemble splits into two or more distinct contingents. One group enters the performance space from stage left while the matching group advances from stage right. Moving in coordination, the groups draw toward each other across the performance ground until meeting in the center, where they merge seamlessly into one or more unified rows. Once the formation consolidates, the movement vocabulary narrows to minimalist, tightly controlled articulations. The torso and lower body remain stationary and erect, with only an occasional stepping action or transition into kneeling. The entire communicative and aesthetic weight rests upon the subtle, supple shaping of the hands and the delicate tilting and turning of the head.

The vocal chants associated with the ula span centuries, reflecting shifting historical eras from ancient compositions to early twentieth-century poetic suites. Older verses such as 'ʻOiau, siʻa langi ula' and references to chiefs such as 'Laulau tuʻi Vaea ē' provide rhythmic and poetic anchorage, while twentieth-century verses celebrate the art form itself with repeated refrains of 'tulituli faiva, he tuli faiva ē' and lines invoking the poetic recitation and gesture ('ʻo lau taʻanga pea fola haka'). These sung texts accompany the ensemble, maintaining a steady vocalized tempo while the dancers trace their arm movements in strict accord with the words.

In terms of presentation and setting, the ula traditionally followed the seated or kneeling ʻotuhaka dance within customary performance sequences. Dancers wear garments closely resembling the attire of the tauʻolunga, though for the ula, vivid red dress is the most popular choice. While the tauʻolunga eventually supplanted it as Tonga's predominant female dance form, the ula survives today as a living connection to the pre-modern court and ceremonial dance repertoires of the island kingdom.

sections.origins_and_history: The ula is an ancient Tongan group dance whose antiquity is attested by early European navigators, including Captain James Cook, who recorded it during eighteenth-century voyages to the Friendly Islands. Prior to the arrival of Christianity, the ula stood as Tonga's primary dance performed by women. Originally executed at a brisk, fast pace with prominent movement of the hips, legs, feet, and upper body, the dance underwent an intentional, radical transformation by the Tongan royal family following Christian conversion. Royal decrees and court aesthetics neutralized its overt hip articulations, establishing a stiff, conservative style that has carried through to contemporary practice, even as its descendant form, the tauʻolunga, grew more popular.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed almost exclusively by girls, with boys joining only on rare occasions. The hallmark structure that gives the dance its alternate name—fahaʻi-ula, or split dance—lies in its entrance: the ensemble divides into two or more contingents, with one half entering from the left and the other from the right. The groups converge in the center of the performance space, merging into one or more horizontal rows. Once in formation, the physical vocabulary becomes intentionally restricted. The torso remains rigid and still, and the legs are rarely used except for occasional steps or shifts into kneeling. Almost all expressive work is concentrated in creating supple, beautiful postures through delicate movements of the hands and precise angling of the head.
sections.music_and_instruments: The musical accompaniment for the ula centers on vocal poetry and chanted texts. Chants preserved from older eras include invocations such as 'ʻOiau, siʻa langi ula; ʻi ʻiē / fai mai siʻa tauʻolunga. ʻio!' and lines honouring leaders such as 'Laulau tuʻi Vaea ē, / Vaea lau mānaʻia.' By the early twentieth century, newer chanted suites were introduced, characterized by repetitive rhythmic verses celebrating performance: 'Tonga, Tonga ē, / tulituli faiva, he tuli faiva ē / peʻi kau muʻa peʻi kau mai / ke tau kalofi kuo tau e langi / tulituli faiva, he tuli faiva ē.' Specific musical instrumentation beyond the vocal chants is not described in sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers dress in attire identical in structure to that worn for the tauʻolunga, though red dress is distinctly favored and most popular for the ula. The setting typically places the dance within a larger ceremonial order: traditionally, the ula is performed immediately after an ʻotuhaka.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Traditionally scheduled after the ʻotuhaka, the ula functions as a formal group dance expressing royal and communal poetry through synchronized gesture. Before Christian missionization transformed Tongan social aesthetics, it served as the foremost female dance expression across the kingdom.
sections.notable_figures: Captain James Cook noted and reported the dance during his early European explorations of Tonga. Historic poetic texts linked to the dance explicitly memorialize noble figures such as Tuʻi Vaea ('Laulau tuʻi Vaea ē, / Vaea lau mānaʻia').
sections.regional_variants: The dance is also known by the variant name fahaʻi-ula (split dance), which may be contracted or degenerated into fahaʻiula, referring to the splitting and converging stage entrance. Additional regional variants are noted to exist, but their specific geographic distinctions are not described in sources.
sections.lineage: The ula is an ancestral group dance from which the widely known Tongan tauʻolunga developed as a direct descendant, ultimately replacing the ula as the kingdom's preeminent female dance.

basic_steps: Divide the ensemble into two flanking groups offstage to the left and right
Process inward toward center stage until lines meet and merge into a single row
Assume an upright, stiff torso posture with minimal leg movement
Execute subtle, supple hand postures in coordination with head tilts while holding a seated, standing, or occasional kneeling posture
teaching.rhythm: Chanted verse rhythm; metric counts not described in sources
teaching.formation: Two or more flanking groups that enter from left and right and merge into one or more rows
teaching.level_notes: Beginners focus on the spatial convergence and holding torso stillness while coordinating wrist and hand postures with head inclinations.

claims.text: The ula is an ancient Tongan group dance that was documented by early European explorers, including Captain Cook.
The dance is also known as fahaʻi-ula, meaning split dance, which can degenerate to fahaʻiula.
Historically, the ula was performed sequentially after an ʻotuhaka performance.
Although less popular than the tauʻolunga that descended from it, the ula continues to be danced today.
Prior to Christianity, the ula was the primary female dance and featured energetic hip, leg, foot, and torso movement at a fast pace.
Following the introduction of Christianity, the Tongan royal family altered the dance to make its movement stiff and conservative.
The split dance title derives from groups entering from the left and right wings before merging in the center into rows.
Performers are girls, with boys participating only rarely.
Most aesthetic expression in the dance is produced by supple postures of the hands and head while the body remains stiff.
Costuming matches tauʻolunga attire, with red garments being the most popular choice.

music_profile.vocal_style: Poetic group chanting with call-and-response refrain lines
music_profile.musical_form: Sequential poetic stanzas with recurring refrains (e.g., 'tulituli faiva, he tuli faiva ē')
music_profile.sound_description: The sonic texture is built on vocalized Tongan chants, featuring rhythmic vocal delivery, collective affirmation syllables, and recurring ancestral poetry sung by an accompanying choir or the dancers themselves.

movement_profile.posture: Stiff, conservative, upright body posture with suppressed hip and upper body swaying
movement_profile.footwork: Minimal lower-body involvement; occasional steps or lowering to a kneeling position
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Supple, beautiful hand gestures (fola haka) that carry the primary artistic and narrative expression
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Stiff torso kept deliberately stationary; hip movement historically present but eliminated following Christian royal intervention
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Bilateral entrance from stage left and stage right, converging at the center into one or more parallel lines
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Stately and restrained in modern execution; historically fast paced

signature_moves.name: Fahaʻi entry
signature_moves.description: Ensemble splits into wings and enters from left and right to merge into unified central lines

signature_moves.name: Haka hand shaping
signature_moves.description: Supple, expressive posturing of the hands executed while keeping the torso stiff

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Ground level; primarily standing with occasional kneeling, no jumps
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid exaggerated hip movement or loose upper-body swaying, which were explicitly banned by royal reforms in favor of conservative stiffness

episode_brief.logline: How a royal decree transformed an ancient, fast-paced Tongan spectacle into an exquisite art of hands, heads, and red dresses.

seniors.seated_version: Perform the entire sequence seated upright on a chair, executing the supple hand movements and head tilts while omitting the marching entrance and kneeling transitions.
seniors.standing_version: Stand in place without traversing the stage, holding the erect torso posture and practicing the hand and head gestures with support nearby if needed.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Maintain a gentle, measured tempo with reduced range in wrist extension to avoid joint strain.
seniors.counts: Counted in steady 4-count or 8-count phrase cycles matching recited chant lines.

children.game_version: The Mirror River game: two equal teams start on opposite sides of the room, walk slowly toward the center tape line to make one straight row, then freeze like statues while moving only their hands and heads.
children.counts: Simple 4-count steps forward followed by 8-count hand posturing.
